how-much-does-whatnot-take-on-a-pallet.h.text:
← Back to the Whatnot payout calculator

How much does Whatnot take on a pallet sale?

Whatnot's pallet/wholesale category is not a smaller version of the collectibles rows. It is 4% commission with no cap at all — a different rate and a different shape from the 8%-up-to-$1,500 row that comics, TCG, sports singles, toys & hobbies, and coins get. Assume the cap carries over from a collectibles show into a pallet lot and the arithmetic is wrong in the direction that costs money on a big lot.

The formula, same as every Whatnot lot

commission = commission rate × hammer — the pallet row has no cap, so the whole hammer is commissioned, not just a slice of it.

processing = 2.9% × (hammer + shipping charged + tax) + $0.30

payout = hammer − commission − processing

Worked example: a $2,000 pallet

No shipping, no tax, the published 4% pallet rate, 2.9% + $0.30 processing.

LineAmount
Hammer$2,000.00
Commission (4% of $2,000, no cap)$80.00
Processing (2.9% of $2,000 + $0.30)$58.30
Total fees$138.30
Payout$1,861.70

Effective take on the hammer: 6.92% — below the 8% headline rate because there is no fixed per-lot fee doing the opposite work a low-dollar collectible sees, just a flat percentage plus the usual processing.

Where the uncapped 4% row stops being the cheaper one

A $6,000 pallet at the pallet rate is $240.00 commission (4% of the full $6,000 — still no cap). The same $6,000 hammer under the capped 8% TCG/comics rate would be commissioned on only the first $1,500 of it, which is $120.00 — half as much, because everything past $1,500 is 0% under that cap. Processing is identical either way ($174.30) since it runs on the checkout total, not the commission base.

The crossover is around $3,000: below it, 4% of the whole hammer is less than 8% of the first $1,500; above it, the capped row wins because it stops taking a cut and the flat 4% never does. A pallet flipper pricing a large mixed lot is comparing a flat rate against a rate with a ceiling, not two flavors of the same shape.

Do this with your own pallet

The Whatnot seller payout calculator ships a "Pallets (wholesale)" category preset that sets the 4%-no-cap rate for you — pick it from the category dropdown and run your own hammer, shipping, and cost. Nothing you type leaves your browser.

Common questions

How much does Whatnot take on a pallet sale?

On the published US pallet/wholesale row, a $2,000 pallet with no shipping or tax is $80.00 commission (4% of $2,000, no cap) plus $58.30 processing (2.9% of $2,000 + $0.30) = $138.30 in fees and a $1,861.70 payout. That is 6.92% of the hammer, not the 8% the standard row headlines.

Does the $1,500 cap apply to pallets?

No. Whatnot's published US wholesale/pallet rate is 4% with no cap at all — the 0%-above-$1,500 shape is published for comics, TCG, sports singles, toys & hobbies, and coins, not for pallets. A pallet lot is commissioned on its full hammer no matter the price.

Is a lower uncapped rate always cheaper than a capped one?

Not past the cap. A $6,000 pallet at the uncapped 4% rate pays $240.00 commission. The same $6,000 hammer at the capped 8% TCG rate pays commission on only the first $1,500, which is $120.00 — half as much. Below roughly $3,000 the 4% uncapped row is cheaper; above it, the 8%-capped row is, because the cap stops taking a cut on everything past $1,500 and the flat 4% never stops.

No warranty. This page is free arithmetic, not legal, tax, financial, or selling advice. Rates change and this is not a comparison against any other category being the "right" one to list under. Verify every figure against your own Whatnot payout statement before you price a pallet.

how-much-does-whatnot-take.html.text:
← Back to the Whatnot payout calculator

How much does Whatnot take per sale?

Whatnot publishes two fees, not one. Commission is a percentage of the item’s final sale price — the hammer. Processing is 2.9% + $0.30 of the checkout total, which is the hammer plus whatever the buyer paid for shipping and tax. A page that says “Whatnot takes 8%” is describing the first line and silently dropping the second.

The formula

commission = commission rate × min(hammer, cap) — no cap means the whole hammer.

processing = 2.9% × (hammer + shipping charged + tax) + $0.30

payout = hammer − commission − processing

That last line is Whatnot’s own “net earnings” definition. Shipping the buyer paid is not added to payout; it is there to cover the label. Leftover after your costs is payout + shipping charged − label − what the lot cost you.

Worked example 1: Whatnot’s own $50 sale

No shipping, no tax, 8% commission, 2.9% + $0.30 processing — the numbers on Whatnot’s US help article.

LineAmount
Hammer$50.00
Commission (8% of $50)$4.00
Processing (2.9% of $50 + $0.30)$1.75
Total fees$5.75
Payout$44.25

Effective take on the hammer: 11.5%, not 8%.

Worked example 2: a $20 TCG card with $5 postage

The lot most live-sellers actually run. Same 8% + 2.9% + $0.30.

LineAmount
Hammer$20.00
Buyer-paid shipping$5.00
Commission (8% of $20)$1.60
Processing (2.9% of $25 + $0.30)$1.03
Total fees$2.63
Payout$17.38

Effective take on the hammer: 13.1%. Of the $1.03 processing, $0.15 is from the postage. That slice is why “just charge shipping” is not free, and why the free-shipping comparison exists.

Worked example 3: a $2,400 graded lot under the $1,500 cap

On the published US comics / TCG / sports / toys row, commission is 8% only up to $1,500. The $900 above the cap is 0%.

Commission is $120.00, not 8% of $2,400 ($192). Processing on $2,400 with no shipping is $69.90. Total fees $189.90, payout $2,210.10. The cap kept $72.00 that a flat 8% page would have taken. The cap is labelled limited-time — confirm it on the lot.

Do this with your own lots

The Whatnot seller payout calculator runs this same arithmetic on your own hammer, postage, tax, label, and cost, with category presets you can overwrite from your statement. Nothing you type leaves your browser.

Common questions

How much does Whatnot take on a $50 sale?

On Whatnot’s published US default, a $50 hammer with no shipping or tax is $4.00 commission (8%) plus $1.75 processing (2.9% of $50 + $0.30) = $5.75 in fees and a $44.25 payout. That is Whatnot’s own worked example.

Does Whatnot charge processing on shipping?

Yes. Processing is 2.9% + $0.30 of the checkout total — hammer plus buyer-paid shipping and tax — not of the hammer alone. A $20 card with $5 postage is $1.60 commission + $1.03 processing = $2.63, 13.1% of the hammer, not 8%.

Does the $1,500 cap apply to every category?

No. Whatnot’s published US help article applies the 0%-above-$1,500 rule to comics, TCG, sports singles, toys & hobbies, and coins. Other categories still commission the whole hammer. The cap is labelled limited-time; confirm it on the lot.

No warranty. This page is free arithmetic, not legal, tax, financial, or selling advice. Rates change. Verify every figure against your own Whatnot payout statement before you price a show.

should-i-offer-free-shipping-on-whatnot..text:
← Back to the Whatnot payout calculator

Should I offer free shipping on Whatnot?

Three ways to handle a label on the same lot. They do not pay the same, because Whatnot’s two fees sit on different bases: commission is on the hammer, processing is on the checkout total.

A $25 lot, an $8 cost, a $5 label

US default rates: 8% commission, 2.9% + $0.30 processing. Same label cost in every column.

Charge $5 postageBake into a $30 hammerEat the label at $25
Hammer$25.00$30.00$25.00
Buyer-paid shipping$5.00$0.00$0.00
Checkout total$30.00$30.00$25.00
Commission$2.00$2.40$2.00
Processing$1.17$1.17$1.03
Payout$21.83$26.43$21.98
Leftover after label + $8 cost$13.83$13.43$8.98

Charging postage wins this lot by $0.40 over baking it in, and by $4.85 over eating the label. Baking the $5 into the hammer puts that $5 on the commission base — 8% of $5 is the 40 cents. Eating the label at the same hammer loses the $5 collected and only saves 2.9% of $5 ($0.15) in processing.

When free shipping can still be the right call

This is arithmetic on one lot, not a rule for a show. Free shipping can still be worth it when a buyer will not bid without it, when a Whatnot promo requires it, or when the alternative is a no-sale. The table above is what that promo costs on this lot, so you can decide whether the extra bid is worth $4.85 — or whether you can raise the start by more than the $5 and still come out ahead of eating it.

Do this with your own label

The Whatnot seller payout calculator has a “Compare free shipping” button that reruns the same lot with buyer-paid shipping zeroed, so you can see the leftover delta on your own hammer and label. Nothing you type leaves your browser.

Common questions

Should I offer free shipping on Whatnot?

Usually no, not at the same hammer. Eating a $5 label on a $25 lot drops leftover by about $4.85 versus charging the buyer that $5 — you lose the postage collected and only save 2.9% of it in processing. Baking the $5 into a $30 hammer is closer, but commission then takes 8% of the postage too.

Is it cheaper to bake shipping into the start price?

No. Commission is on the hammer only. A $25 lot with $5 buyer-paid shipping and a $5 label leftover $13.83 after an $8 cost. The same lot started at $30 with free shipping leftover $13.43 — 40 cents less, which is 8% of the $5 you moved onto the hammer. Processing is the same because the checkout total is $30 either way.

No warranty. This page is free arithmetic, not legal, tax, financial, or selling advice. It does not tell you what to start a lot at. Verify every figure against your own Whatnot payout statement.

vs-tracking-payouts-in-a-spreadsheet.htm.text:
← Whatnot Seller Payout Calculator

Whatnot Seller Payout Calculator vs. tracking payouts in a spreadsheet

A seller who runs more than one Whatnot show usually ends up with a spreadsheet: a cell for the commission rate, one for the $1,500 category cap, a processing formula on the checkout total, and a new row whenever the show mixes categories — a TCG lot at 8% up to the cap, a coin roll at 4%, a pallet at 4% with no cap at all. Each formula is ordinary arithmetic. Remembering which cap applies to which lot, and re-deriving the free-shipping tradeoff every time a buyer asks, is the part that gets skipped when the next lot is already live.

What each approach actually does

A spreadsheet can reproduce every formula this calculator runs — commission on the hammer, the $1,500 cap by category, processing on item plus buyer-paid shipping and tax plus $0.30, and the charge-it / bake-it-in / eat-it free-shipping comparison. Building it means typing Whatnot's published rates into the right cells and adding a cap check for every category the show touches, then updating it whenever Whatnot's published rates change.

This calculator keeps the four category presets, the cap, and the free-shipping comparison on one screen, so a TCG lot near $1,500 and a no-cap pallet in the same show use the same worksheet instead of two. A shareable link carries the full scenario in the URL, so a number checked on a phone mid-show is the same link opened on a laptop afterward.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What's left after commission and processing on this lot?This calculator's payout panel — one screen, the right cap applied.
Does charging for shipping or baking it into the price leave more?This calculator's free-shipping comparison, not a third spreadsheet tab.
My situation has a wrinkle this calculator doesn't model (a bundled lot, a promo credit).A spreadsheet you build yourself — it can represent any rule you can describe.
I want the hammer bid a resale lot needs to hit a target payout.This calculator's target-leftover mode, solved for you instead of goal-seeked by hand.
Is my data uploaded anywhere?No. Everything runs in your browser; your figures stay on this device.

Common questions

Can a spreadsheet do this math instead?

Yes. Commission on the hammer, the $1,500 cap on TCG/comics/sports/coins, processing on the checkout total (item plus buyer-paid shipping and tax) plus $0.30, and the free-shipping comparison are all ordinary arithmetic you can put in a spreadsheet. Building it means copying Whatnot's published rates into the right cells and remembering to re-check the cap on every lot near $1,500, category by category.

What does a spreadsheet not do that this calculator does?

Apply the category cap for you. A spreadsheet formula that charges commission on the full hammer keeps overstating the fee on every graded card, coin roll, or sports lot over $1,500 until someone notices and patches the cell — this calculator applies the cap by category preset, so a $2,400 graded lot is never charged as if the cap didn't exist. It also runs the charge-it / bake-it-in / eat-it free-shipping comparison in one view and produces a shareable link that carries the whole lot instead of a file to keep in sync between a phone during a live show and a laptop afterward.

Is a spreadsheet ever the better choice?

Yes, when your situation has a wrinkle this calculator does not model — a bundled multi-item lot, a promo credit, or a fee structure from a plan this tool's inputs cannot represent. A spreadsheet you build yourself can represent any rule you can describe. This calculator trades that flexibility for a form that already has the right fields and the right cap for a single lot moving through a standard Whatnot sale.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No. The calculator runs entirely in your browser. A shareable link carries your numbers in the URL itself rather than sending them to a server, and the optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your prices or costs.

vs-whatnot-seller-dashboard.html.text:
← Whatnot seller payout calculator

This calculator vs. Whatnot's own fee schedule and payout statement

Whatnot publishes a seller fee schedule and, after a show, sends you a payout statement listing what each order actually earned and what was actually deducted. Those are the authoritative numbers. They are what you were charged, and every figure on this page should be checked against them.

But a statement only exists after a lot has sold, and a schedule is a set of rates rather than an answer about your lot. This page answers the narrower, earlier question: for a lot you have not listed yet, at a hammer you are considering, what would actually be left — with no account, no show, and nothing uploaded.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What was I actually charged on the lots that sold in last night's show? Whatnot's own payout statement — authoritative, and the figure to check this page against.
What are the current commission and processing rates for my category and region? Whatnot's published fee schedule. The presets here are labelled starting points copied from a help article; they expire.
For a lot I have not listed yet, at a hammer I am considering, what is left after fees, the label, and what the lot cost me? This calculator — type the figures, get an answer immediately, before the show.
Is 2.9% processing being charged on the buyer's postage and tax as well as the item? This calculator prices processing on the whole checkout total, which is what a flat "Whatnot takes 8%" page hides.
Is it cheaper to charge shipping or to eat the label myself? This calculator's free-shipping comparison — it depends on the hammer and the label, not on a rule of thumb.
What hammer would this lot need to clear a leftover target? This calculator's target solver, which works backwards from the leftover you want.
How does the $1,500 category cap change a high-value graded lot? This calculator's commission cap input — the portion above the cap commissions at 0%, so 8% of the whole hammer is the wrong number.
Price a lot now

This tool needs no account and no Whatnot login: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and your hammers, costs, and leftovers stay on this device — nothing is uploaded anywhere. It cannot read your orders or your real statement, which is why every rate on it is an editable input rather than a live feed.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Whatnot's own numbers?

Both, at different moments. Whatnot's published fee schedule and the payout statement you receive after a show are authoritative — they are what you were actually charged, and every figure here should be checked against them. But a statement only exists once a lot has already sold, and the schedule is a set of rates rather than an answer about your lot. This page is a single static form for the moment before that: you type a hammer, what the lot cost you, the label, and any buyer-paid shipping or tax, and it prints what would be left — no account, no show, no sale required.

Whatnot publishes a worked example. Why is that not enough?

Whatnot's help material carries a worked example of a $50 sale costing $5.75 in fees. It is correct and it is one lot. It does not show a $20 TCG card with $5 of buyer-paid shipping, where 2.9% payment processing applies to the whole checkout total — item plus postage plus tax — rather than to the hammer alone, so the effective take is not 8% of $20. It also does not show a $2,400 graded lot, where the published $1,500 commission cap on selected categories means the portion above $1,500 commissions at 0%. This page runs the same arithmetic against your figures instead of a fixed example.

Does this page connect to my Whatnot seller account?

No. There is no account, no login, no linking, and no upload. It is a static page: the arithmetic runs in your own browser, and the hammers, costs, and leftovers you type stay on your device. It cannot read your orders, submit a listing, or see your real statement — which is exactly why the rates on it are editable inputs rather than a live feed.

Are the preset rates current?

Treat them as labelled starting points, not as a live schedule. They come from a published help article, they change, and they vary by region and category. Every rate on the page is an editable input for that reason: replace the preset with the line on your own payout statement, and the arithmetic follows your number rather than ours.

Is this page affiliated with Whatnot?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Whatnot Inc. Whatnot is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this calculator is for.

How much does Whatnot take on a $2,400 graded card?

Not 8% of $2,400. On the published US row for comics, TCG, sports singles and toys & hobbies, commission is 8% of the first $1,500 of the hammer and 0% on the rest. Processing is separate and has no cap. Price a big lot with a flat 8% and you overstate the fee by $72.

commission = 8% × min(hammer, $1,500)

processing = 2.9% × (hammer + shipping charged + tax) + $0.30

Effective take on the hammer: 7.91%. A flat 8% commission would give $192.00 commission, $261.90 in fees (10.91%) and a $2,138.10 payout.

The cap only helps above $1,500

At $800 the same row is $64.00 commission + $23.50 processing = $87.50 (10.94% of the hammer). At $1,500 it is $120.00 + $43.80 = $163.80 (10.92%). At $5,000 commission is still $120.00, so fees are $265.30 (5.31%). Commission stops growing at $1,500; processing never stops.

How much does Whatnot take on a $2,400 graded card?

That is 7.91% of the hammer, not the $192.00 commission a flat 8% would suggest.

Is the $1,500 commission cap permanent?

No. Whatnot publishes it as a limited-time US shape and it varies by category and region, so treat it as an input, not a fact. The calculator's category presets are starting points: replace the rate and cap with the line on your own payout statement.

Does the cap lower the processing fee too?

No. Processing is 2.9% + $0.30 of what the buyer paid at checkout (item, shipping and tax) and the commission cap does not touch it. On the $2,400 lot processing is $69.90 either way; the cap saves $72.00 of commission only.
